The Invisible Ledger: Quantifying the Invisible Wedge in Indonesia's Platform Economy

研究生 / Student: 王新福 Christopher Ongko
指導教授 / Advisor: 孔德蓉 De-Rong Kong
中華民國 115 年 9 月
September 2026

Abstract
The digital economy is measured through several indicators (platform transaction value, platform
revenue, national e-commerce statistics and payment data) that capture different parts of the same
activity but are often used interchangeably. This study asks how much economic activity remains
invisible when digital platforms are measured through their reported revenue, and when that choice
changes the conclusion about growth. Between 2022 and 2023, Tokopedia's revenue rose 53.2
percent while its transaction value fell 8.9 percent. Among Indonesian platforms reporting both
figures, revenue grew faster in six of eight year-to-year comparisons, by a margin significantly larger
than among listed platforms outside Indonesia. Nationally, most e-commerce growth came from
more participating businesses, and 98.5 percent of 2023–2024 growth lay outside the marketplace
channel of BPS-Statistics Indonesia. Conclusions about scale and growth therefore depend on the
indicator used.

1. Introduction
Between 2022 and 2023, Tokopedia's revenue rose 53.2 percent while the transaction value it
processed fell 8.9 percent: read through its accounts, the platform was expanding quickly; read
through its transactions, it was shrinking. Both figures come from the same company's disclosures.
Of the increase in net revenue, 60.6 percent reconciles to lower customer incentives, the partner
incentives and end-user promotions that GoTo deducts from gross revenue to arrive at net revenue
(GoTo Gojek Tokopedia 2024), and 39.4 percent to higher gross revenue. The reversal is not
isolated: among the three platforms that report both figures themselves, revenue grew faster than
transaction value in six of eight year-to-year comparisons between 2020 and 2025, and in two of
these the measures moved in opposite directions.
The same gap runs through the wider digital economy. Southeast Asia's digital economy grew from
approximately US$100 billion in 2020 to US$263 billion in 2024 (Google, Temasek and Bain 2020,
2024). That figure is one indicator of the activity: the gross value of the transactions involved. Digital
platforms, which carry many of those transactions, report a different number, their own revenue;
national statistical agencies report a third, the online sales of surveyed businesses; and payment
systems report a fourth, the value of funds moved. The indicators are designed to measure different
things, yet they are often used interchangeably, and substituting one for another changes the
measured scale, growth and even the direction of digital activity.
Suppose a platform processes 100 units of transaction value but recognizes only 10 as its own
revenue: the commissions and fees it earns for arranging the transactions. Depending on the business
model, the remaining 90 can include merchant receipts, driver payouts, inventory costs, taxes and
other pass-through payments. An analyst using the platform's accounts sees 10, while one measuring
the commerce it processes sees 100. I call the difference the invisible wedge (W). The term refers to
what a revenue-only measure excludes, not to unrecorded activity. Revenue records what the
platform earned, while transaction value records what it carried. Platform economics and revenuerecognition rules explain why such a gap exists (Rochet and Tirole 2003; Hagiu and Wright 2015;
Evans and Schmalensee 2016; International Accounting Standards Board 2014), but there is little
evidence on how large it becomes in practice or whether it stays stable enough for revenue to stand
in for the commerce a platform carries.
Against this backdrop, I study Indonesia, the largest digital market in Southeast Asia. Platform
reports disclose both the commerce a platform carries and the revenue it recognizes, so the
consequences of substituting one for the other can be observed directly within the same accounts.
The study covers four marketplaces, including Tokopedia, Blibli, Bukalapak and Shopee, and Grab,
whose Indonesian business is mainly delivery and other on-demand services. Tokopedia, Blibli
and Bukalapak report both measures themselves (i.e., issuer-reported figures). For Grab and Shopee,
Indonesian figures must be constructed from company-wide ratios and a third-party estimate. 1 To
limit the concerns this raises, I follow each platform against itself through time and keep issuerreported and constructed figures apart, so that the company, the business activity and the reporting
convention stay as constant as the disclosures allow. I then compare the platform evidence with two
independent indicators: national e-commerce statistics from BPS-Statistics Indonesia (BPS), the
national statistical agency, and payment statistics from Bank Indonesia, the central bank. Only
platform transaction value and revenue enter the wedge; BPS and payment data serve as comparison
indicators with their own definitions and scope.
In 2023, Tokopedia, Shopee and Grab together processed US$43.23 billion of transaction value
against US$3.16 billion of recognized revenue, a wedge of US$40.07 billion. The wedge establishes
scale; the central question is whether revenue remains a stable guide to the commerce underneath it,

and, as Tokopedia shows, it need not. National statistics show the same problem one level up. BPS
classifies each surveyed business's online sales by the channel used, such as marketplaces, social
media, instant messaging or its own website. It places the 2023 marketplace component of ecommerce at about US$13.2 billion, below the transaction value of either Tokopedia or Shopee
alone, and reports that 98.5 percent of the increase in e-commerce value between 2023 and 2024
came from outside its marketplace category. Payment measures from Bank Indonesia grew between
1.8 and 11 times as fast as e-commerce value.
One concern is that some of the Indonesian figures are constructed rather than reported by the
platforms (Grab and Shopee). I address this in three ways. First, the growth analysis uses only the
platforms that report both transaction value and revenue themselves. Second, I vary the monetization
rate assumed for Shopee. Third, I compare the Indonesian platforms with eight listed platforms
outside Indonesia: revenue also grew faster in 22 of 29 comparisons there, but the median divergence
was 7.10 percentage points, against 38.92 in Indonesia, a difference that is statistically significant
(Section 5.1).
A statement about how large Indonesia's digital economy is, or how fast it grew, is therefore a
statement about an indicator. The choice matters to investors, who value platforms largely on
reported revenue; to statistical agencies sizing the digital economy; and to tax authorities, which
increasingly rely on marketplace records to identify sellers and their transactions (Ministry of
Finance of the Republic of Indonesia 2025; Business Times 2026). An investor relying on platform
revenue and an analyst relying on marketplace figures can reach opposite conclusions about the
same years because the indicators measure different objects.
1.1 Research question and objectives
One question drives the proposal: How much economic activity remains invisible when digital
platforms are measured through their reported revenue, and when does that choice change the
conclusion about growth? Indonesia provides the main empirical setting. Three objectives of this
study follow. First, I measure the invisible wedge across the platform histories available from 2020
to 2025. Second, I reconcile selected large movements with disclosed changes in monetization,
customer incentives, revenue recognition and reporting scope. Third, I compare the platform
evidence with national e-commerce and payment indicators to test whether they give the same
account of economic scale and growth.
A separate comparison of eight listed platform businesses outside Indonesia, such as eBay and
Mercado Libre, tests whether the separation between transaction value and revenue appears under
other business models.
1.2 Contributions
My study contributes to the literature in several ways. First, I extend the literature on digital
platforms. Platform economics and revenue-recognition research explain why a gap between
transaction value and revenue exists and can move (Rochet and Tirole 2003; Hagiu and Wright 2015;
International Accounting Standards Board 2014), but not how large it becomes in practice. I turn the
invisible wedge from a one-year estimate into a measure tracked over time. Revenue is not a stable
guide to the commerce behind it: among the issuer-reported platforms, revenue outgrew transaction
value in six of eight comparisons, and in two of these the measures moved in opposite directions.
Second, I reconcile a major movement in the wedge using accounting components the platform
discloses. Of the increase in Tokopedia's net revenue between 2022 and 2023, 60.6 percent
reconciles to lower customer incentives and 39.4 percent to higher gross revenue, even though its
transaction value fell that year.

Third, I extend the comparison beyond company accounts, in line with official frameworks that
distinguish the commerce facilitated through a platform from the platform's own service (Ahmad
and Schreyer 2016; OECD 2023). National statistics and payment indicators disagree with the
platform picture, and with each other, about both the level and the growth of Indonesian digital
commerce.
Finally, I address a measurement problem in finance. Platform reports reveal both the commerce a
platform carries and the revenue it recognizes, allowing the consequences of substituting one
measure for the other to be observed directly. De Franco, Kothari and Verdi (2011) show why
comparable accounting bases matter, while Berg et al. (2020) show that intermediary-held digital
traces contain information conventional records can miss. Studies of internet firms also find that
activity measures carry information beyond reported revenue (Trueman, Wong and Zhang 2001;
Rajgopal, Venkatachalam and Kotha 2003). This study applies those ideas to platform economies
and shows that the indicator chosen to describe digital activity changes the economic conclusion.
2. Literature Review
Digital platforms sit between economic activity and the indicators used to measure it. They facilitate
transactions between buyers and sellers, recognize only part of that activity as their own revenue,
and generate records that can also appear in payment, statistical, and administrative systems.
Existing research explains each part of this process from a different angle. Taken together, it provides
the foundation for asking how much activity remains invisible when platforms are measured through
reported revenue.
2.1 Platform Economics and Revenue Recognition
Platform economics explains why the value of commerce processed through a platform can be much
larger than the revenue the platform records. Digital platforms often connect consumers with
merchants or other service providers and earn commissions, fees, advertising, logistics, or other
intermediation revenue rather than the full value of every transaction they facilitate (Rochet and
Tirole 2003; Caillaud and Jullien 2003; Parker and Van Alstyne 2005; Armstrong 2006; Hagiu and
Wright 2015; Evans and Schmalensee 2016).
In particular, revenue-recognition rules affect how much of this difference appears in the accounts.
Under International Financial Reporting Standard 15 (IFRS 15), whether a company acts as a
principal or an agent affects whether it recognizes the full customer payment or only the amount it
earns from arranging the transaction (International Accounting Standards Board 2014). Customer
incentives, monetization, service mix, acquisitions, and changes in business scope can also move
reported revenue without an equivalent change in transaction activity. De Franco, Kothari and Verdi
(2011) show why comparable accounting bases matter when financial information is interpreted.
Overall, the literature explains why a transaction–revenue gap can exist and move over time, but not
how economically large that gap becomes in practice.
2.2 Measuring the Digital Economy
Official measurement frameworks already distinguish between the commerce facilitated through a
platform and the service provided by the platform itself. National-accounting guidance separates the
buyer-seller transaction from the platform's intermediation service rather than treating the full
transaction value as platform output (Ahmad and Schreyer 2016; International Monetary Fund 2018;
OECD 2023; United Nations et al. 2025).
In practice, the quantities are published by different producers. For instance, industry reports size
the regional digital economy by gross merchandise value (Google, Temasek and Bain 2024), national
statistics measure the online sales of surveyed businesses (BPS-Statistics Indonesia 2025), and listed
platforms report the revenue they recognize under IFRS 15 (International Accounting Standards

Board 2014). A difference that is harmless when the measures move together becomes important
when they do not, because the choice of measure can change conclusions about economic scale and
growth. Overall, this study treats substitution between indicators as a question to be tested, as
research on night-time lights does for measured income (Henderson, Storeygard and Weil 2012).
2.3 Digital Records and Third-Party Information
Transactions that do not enter a platform's revenue can still leave detailed records within the
platform's system. Merchants and service providers can be small, self-employed, or weakly
represented in conventional financial records, yet the transactions they make on a platform are
recorded by it. This differs from shadow-economy settings, where reliable formal records may be
sparse (La Porta and Shleifer 2014; Ulyssea 2018; Medina and Schneider 2019). Platform-mediated
activity can also create traces outside conventional records (Berg et al. 2020; Barrios, Hochberg and
Yi 2022; Denes, Lagaras and Tsoutsoura 2025).
Third-party information changes compliance and enforcement (Kleven et al. 2011; Pomeranz 2015;
Naritomi 2019; Kleven, Kreiner and Saez 2016; Slemrod 2019). The Model Rules of the
Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD 2020) and the European Union's
seventh Directive on Administrative Cooperation (DAC7; European Union 2021) apply this
principle to platforms, as does Indonesia's Minister of Finance Regulation No. 37 of 2025 (PMK
37/2025) through seller identification, transaction-linked reporting and marketplace withholding
(Ministry of Finance of the Republic of Indonesia 2025). Overall, the relevance here is
informational: what a measure or rule can show depends on the records it uses.
2.4 Research Gap
Existing research explains the pieces of the problem separately. Platform economics explains why
transaction value can exceed revenue; accounting explains why the gap can move; official
measurement frameworks explain why these quantities should not be treated as equivalent; and
research on digital records explains why some platform-mediated activity outside revenue can
remain observable in platform records.
However, there is a research gap regarding how large these differences become in practice, whether
they persist over time, and whether choosing one indicator instead of another changes the economic
conclusion. This study addresses that gap by measuring the invisible wedge over time, examining
disclosed reasons for major movements, comparing platform accounts with national e-commerce
and payment indicators, and using external platform evidence to test whether the same pattern
appears beyond Indonesia.
3. Theoretical Framework and Hypotheses
Digital platform activity can be observed through several indicators, but those indicators do not
measure the same economic object. The framework begins with the difference between the value a
platform processes and the revenue it recognizes, then asks whether that relationship remains stable
over time and whether other indicators produce the same account of digital activity. Figure 1
illustrates the framework.

Figure 1. Research framework.
For illustrative purposes only; circle sizes are not to scale, and the platform circle is not identical to the marketplace
channel of BPS-Statistics Indonesia, whose definition differs. H1 tests the inner link between revenue and platform
commerce; H2 tests the outer link between platform commerce and national e-commerce growth.

3.1 Measurement Framework
For the platform analysis, transaction value and revenue are paired only when they refer to the same
period and business activity. Figures that issuers report and figures that must be constructed are kept
apart, as are national statistics and payment indicators (Section 4). In my study, I measure the level
of the “invisible wedge,” denoted by W, in currency units as follows:
Wit = Vit − Rit

(1)

where Vit denotes transaction value processed by platform i in period t, and Rit the revenue recognized
over the same matched period and business scope. W represents the invisible wedge, calculated as
the transaction value occurring outside the platform’s recognized revenue. It should not be
interpreted as an accounting omission, as both quantities may be reported within the same company
disclosure. It is a transaction-value measure rather than an income or value-added measure; Section
7 states the corresponding inference boundaries. To account for differences in platform size, I also
report the wedge relative to revenue. Specifically, I define the Ecosystem Ratio (E) as:
Eit = Wit / Rit

(2)

The Ecosystem Ratio is constructed for this study as a descriptive transformation of the monetization
rate, and its interpretation draws on two established results. First, platform economics shows that
booked revenue need not track the transaction value a multisided platform coordinates (Rochet and
Tirole 2003; Hagiu and Wright 2015; Evans and Schmalensee 2016). Second, accounting research
shows that the share of transaction value recognized as revenue depends on how revenue is
recognized, including whether the platform acts as principal or agent (International Accounting
Standards Board 2014; De Franco, Kothari and Verdi 2011). For example, an E of 9 means that nine
units of transaction value remain outside the revenue for every unit that is recognized as platform
revenue. Equivalently, transaction value is ten times revenue, and approximately 10 percent of
transaction value is recognized as revenue.
A single ratio does not show whether the relationship holds through time, so I further define annual
“growth divergence,” denoted by D, as follows:

Dit = g(Rit) − g(Vit)

(3)

where g(X) is the percentage growth of X from one year to the next. A positive D means revenue
grew faster than transaction value, so the platform's monetization rate, m = R/V, rose and E fell; a
negative D means the reverse. Because R = m × V, any divergence between the two growth rates
reflects a change in m (for small changes, D approximates the growth of m), and the same definitions
give E = (V − R)/R = V/R − 1 = 1/m − 1. If revenue were a stable proxy for transaction value, D would
remain close to zero. W gives the wedge in currency units, E expresses it relative to revenue, and D
carries the central test: whether the relationship between revenue and transaction value remains
stable over time.
3.2 Hypothesis Development
Two hypotheses follow from the research question. H1 asks whether revenue tracks the commerce
carried within a platform; H2 asks whether platform records can track the growth of national ecommerce. Together they test the two links between the indicator most often used, platform revenue,
and the activity it is used to represent. Table 1 pairs each hypothesis with its principal test.
Platform economics and accounting both suggest that the share of transaction value a platform
recognizes as revenue is not fixed. Revenue depends on monetization, customer incentives and
whether the platform acts as principal or agent under IFRS 15, and these can change with the
platform's business model, scope and pricing (Rochet and Tirole 2003; Hagiu and Wright 2015;
International Accounting Standards Board 2014). Research on key performance indicators likewise
finds that a disclosed measure becomes less informative when the way it is computed changes over
time (Givoly et al. 2019). Revenue therefore tracks transaction activity only while m stays constant,
that is, while D is close to zero.
If the relationship between transaction value (V) and platform revenue (R) were stable, revenue would
be a workable stand-in for the commerce a platform carries, the growth divergence (D) would remain
close to zero and the Ecosystem Ratio (E) would be constant. Accordingly, I propose the following
hypothesis:
H1. Transaction value and revenue recognized by the same platform grow proportionally over
time.
The test compares the size of D with its size among listed platforms outside Indonesia, where revenue
and transaction value broadly move together (Section 4.5).
National e-commerce value can grow because existing businesses sell more (the intensive margin)
or because more businesses sell online (the extensive margin; Hummels and Klenow 2005). The
distinction matters for measurement: growth driven by new sellers can take place in channels that
platform accounts do not cover, such as social media and instant messaging, which BPS reports are
widely used (BPS-Statistics Indonesia 2025), so platform figures can miss it even when each
platform reports accurately. Because BPS reports both the number of e-commerce businesses and
total e-commerce value, national growth can be divided arithmetically into these two components
(Section 4.4). I therefore hypothesize that:
H2. The growth of national e-commerce value is attributable primarily to an increase in the
number of participating businesses, rather than to higher sales per business.
The split is arithmetic and does not assign new businesses to particular channels. H1 and H2 are
therefore linked: H1 tests whether revenue represents the commerce a platform carries, and H2 tests
whether the commerce platforms carry represents national e-commerce growth.
Two further analyses support these hypotheses without forming separate hypotheses. First, BPS's
split of e-commerce value by sales channel shows whether national growth took place inside or

outside the marketplace channel. Second, BPS's business-level comparison shows whether
marketplace sellers are more likely to keep financial statements, which bears on the information that
platform records can supply to tax administration. Both are reported in Section 5.2 as additional
analyses.

4. Data and Methodology
My study uses several indicators because no single one captures every part of digital platform
activity. Platform reports provide transaction value and revenue; BPS-Statistics Indonesia provides
national e-commerce and business evidence; Bank Indonesia provides payment statistics; and
platform companies outside Indonesia provide a separate comparison.
4.1 Selecting the Platform Evidence
The basic observation is one platform in one year, with transaction value and revenue referring to
the same period and, as closely as possible, the same business activity. An observation is retained
only when its period, geographic and business coverage, units, definitions, and source can be
identified; measures referring to different periods are excluded, and major changes in accounting
definitions or business structure are recorded.
The main sample consists of the platforms that report transaction value and revenue themselves:
Tokopedia, Blibli and Bukalapak. Grab and Shopee, whose Indonesian figures must be constructed,
support the 2023 scale comparison.2 According to 2023 statistics, Shopee and Tokopedia together
accounted for approximately 70 percent of Indonesia’s estimated marketplace transaction value
(Momentum Works 2024; see Section 4.3). Grab, a major delivery intermediary, was also included
in the analysis. As shown in Table 2, the main sample has 11 platform-years and 8 year-to-year
comparisons; adding Grab and Shopee raises these to 17 and 12. Each series covers only years for
which a matched pair exists.3

4.2 Comparing Platform Activity through Time
When transaction value and revenue move sharply apart, disclosed changes in monetization,
customer incentives, revenue recognition, and business scope are used to reconcile the movement
where the filings permit; these reconciliations are arithmetic rather than causal.
Companies use different names for transaction activity, including gross transaction value (GTV),
gross merchandise value (GMV), and total payment volume (TPV). Transaction value, V, is the
umbrella concept in this proposal and is labeled GTV; each issuer's own label and definition is
retained and checked rather than assumed to be identical.4
Growth rates are computed in each issuer's reporting currency, so exchange-rate movements do not
enter D. US dollar values are used only for the 2023 cross-section, where rupiah figures are converted
at the World Bank's 2023 official exchange rate of 15,236.88 rupiah per dollar (World Bank 2026).

digitalization (Bank Indonesia 2025). Because they cover more than e-commerce and also reflect
adoption and substitution between payment methods, they are compared by growth rate and are not
treated as sales estimates.
4.5 External Evidence and Robustness
The external comparison contains 48 matched annual observations for eight listed platform
businesses from 2017 to 2025: eBay, Etsy, Jumia, Mercado Libre, Rakuten, Sea, Shopify and
Zalando. It is reported separately from the Indonesian evidence and serves as the benchmark for
testing H1: a one-sided Mann–Whitney test (Mann and Whitney 1947) compares the absolute
divergence |D| in Indonesia with the 29 comparisons unaffected by acquisitions or changes in
reporting scope, repeated with one median per platform because comparisons within a platform are
not independent.
Robustness checks vary the sample-inclusion rules, revenue definitions, publication versions, and
the assumptions in the constructed country measures. The resulting ranges are reported as sensitivity
ranges rather than statistical confidence intervals.

5. Preliminary Evidence and Feasibility
The evidence assembled so far establishes that the proposed comparisons can be carried out and that
the choice of indicator produces economically meaningful differences. The results first show the
scale and movement of the wedge, then compare the platform picture with national and payment
indicators.
5.1 Platform Scale and Movement
The 2023 comparison covers the three platforms introduced in Section 4.1: Shopee, Tokopedia and
Grab.

Table 5 reports that cross-section. Across the three platforms, US$43.23 billion of transaction value
corresponds to US$3.16 billion of recognized revenue, a wedge of US$40.07 billion and a
transaction-value-to-revenue ratio of 13.7 to 1 (E = 12.7). In terms of economic significance, the
wedge is equivalent in magnitude to about 2.9 percent of Indonesia's 2023 nominal GDP of
US$1.371 trillion (World Bank 2026); the comparison is of magnitude only, since the wedge is
transaction value rather than value added.
One concern is that two ratios rest on construction. Shopee's 9.0 follows from an assumed companywide monetization rate of 10 percent, and Grab's 7.9 is its company-wide ratio, so neither provides
independent Indonesian ratio evidence. To address this concern, I vary Shopee's rate from 9 to 11
percent, which puts the combined wedge between US$39.86 billion and US$40.29 billion, and
exclude each platform in turn, which leaves a wedge of at least US$20.70 billion.
At the 2023 exchange rate, Blibli's and Bukalapak's reported transaction and revenue figures yield
wedges of US$3.20 billion and US$10.50 billion. They are excluded from the total because Blibli's
measure includes online travel and Bukalapak's is reported at Group level. Their ratios, 43.4 and
36.0, sit close to Tokopedia's 39.3; the constructed ratios, by contrast, reflect company-wide
monetization.
The relationship is not stable. Revenue grew faster in six of the eight main-sample comparisons, and
in two comparisons revenue and transaction value moved in opposite directions. Tokopedia's 53.2
percent revenue growth against an 8.9 percent transaction-value decline gives a 62.1-point
divergence. The median absolute divergence, 38.92 percentage points, compares with 7.10 points
outside Indonesia, where revenue growth and transaction-value growth are closely correlated (0.98
excluding Sea, whose Shopee business also operates in Indonesia, against 0.10 in the Indonesian
main sample). A one-sided Mann–Whitney test rejects equal divergence (p = 0.002). The result holds

after dropping the largest comparison, where revenue still grew faster in five of seven (p = 0.006),
when Sea is excluded from the benchmark (p < 0.001), and with one median per platform (p =
0.024). Adding Grab and Shopee raises the count to ten of twelve, but their four comparisons simply
reflect company-wide monetization. The evidence is therefore inconsistent with H1. Table A3 in
Appendix A reports summary statistics for all available comparisons, and Figure 2 shows D for each
main-sample comparison.

Figure 2. Growth divergence D = g(R) − g(V) in the issuer-reported main sample, 2020–2025.
Positive values indicate faster revenue growth; diamonds mark the two sign reversals. Blibli 2022–2023 is shown on a
broken axis.

Tokopedia illustrates the separation. In 2022–2023, transaction value fell 8.9 percent while thirdparty net revenue rose 53.2 percent; 60.6 percent of the revenue increase reconciles to lower
customer incentives and 39.4 percent to higher gross revenue. Its accounts show growth, while its
transactions show contraction. Blibli showed a similar reversal in 2024–2025: transaction value fell
1.89 percent and net revenue rose 12.07 percent. The pattern therefore appears across more than one
platform and period.
5.2 Evidence Beyond Platform Revenue
National statistics give a different account of the same commerce, beginning with its level. BPS
measures online sales reported by surveyed e-commerce businesses; Tokopedia reports GTV, while
the external Shopee figure is a GMV estimate. In its exclusive channel split, where marketplaces
account for 18.2 percent of e-commerce value, BPS places the 2023 marketplace component at
Rp200.68 trillion, about US$13.2 billion. Tokopedia's reported GTV and the external Shopee
estimate together total US$37.9 billion. Because channel attribution and reporting definitions differ,
the indicators are not yet like-for-like. The study will reconcile those definitions before attributing
any part of the difference to coverage.
Growth can be compared more directly. Table 6 summarizes the evidence for H2, the additional
analyses and the payment context.

BPS also reports widespread use of non-marketplace channels. In 2023, 95.33 percent of ecommerce businesses used instant messaging. In its multiple-response measure, where a business
can report several channels, social media accounted for 44.04 percent of transaction value and
marketplaces for 32.74 percent; that measure is not comparable with the exclusive 18.2 percent split
above. These figures describe the 2023 channel structure rather than the allocation of 2023–2024
growth. The business-count split is arithmetic and the recordkeeping result is an association. The
business-count result also holds for 2022–2023, when more businesses account for about 71 percent
of the increase (Table 6). Overall, the BPS evidence is consistent with H2, and the additional
analyses place most national growth outside the marketplace channel, subject to the definitional
differences noted above.
5.3 Feasibility and Scope of the Preliminary Findings
Overall, the preliminary evidence is inconsistent with H1 and consistent with H2: revenue did not
grow in proportion to transaction value within the issuer-reported platforms, and national ecommerce growth came mainly from more participating businesses in both available transitions. The
additional analyses place most of that growth outside the marketplace channel and show that
marketplace sellers are more likely to keep complete financial statements.
Outside Indonesia, transaction value exceeds revenue in all eight businesses. In the latest reported
year, monetization rates range from about 3 percent at Shopify to about 25 percent at Mercado Libre,
and reach about 70 percent at Zalando, whose revenue includes its own retail sales. The level of the
wedge therefore varies widely with the business model even where its growth is stable, which is why
the test of H1 uses growth divergence rather than levels.
PMK 37/2025 provides an administrative example. It designates marketplace operators to report
seller-linked transactions and withhold tax, and its implementation has been deferred. The
designated operators cannot yet be mapped directly to BPS's marketplace category, and compliance
and revenue effects remain outside this study.

6. Why the Problem Matters
Indonesia's digital economy is observed through platform accounts, transaction measures, national
statistics and payment indicators, which disagree about scale and growth. Tokopedia's transaction
value fell 8.9 percent while its revenue rose 53.2 percent, and BPS's marketplace category grew 1.45
percent while all e-commerce grew 17.08 percent. The contribution is to identify which conclusions
depend on the indicator selected, and when revenue ceases to be a stable guide to the commerce a
platform carries. Investors typically value platforms on revenue, while statistical agencies and tax
authorities increasingly work from transaction records; when the two diverge, these users can reach
opposite conclusions about the same activity.
7. Limitations and Robustness
This proposal has several limitations that also suggest avenues for future research. First, the
sample is small. The main sample has three platforms, 11 platform-years and 8 comparisons, so the
formal tests have limited power and rely on an external benchmark that is purposive rather than
random. Second, coverage and scope are uneven: Tokopedia is observed for two years, Blibli
includes online travel, and Bukalapak reports at Group level. Third, Grab's and Shopee's figures are
constructed, their ratios contain no independent Indonesian information, and Shopee's revenue uses
an assumed monetization rate. Finally, Section 5.2 compares indicators with different definitions;
their disagreement is measured but not yet reconciled, and the national evidence covers two annual
transitions for the business-count split and one for the channel split. Future research could add
platforms such as Lazada and TikTok Shop once matched Indonesian revenue series become
available, and could reconcile the definitions behind the BPS and platform levels.

One concern is that the results depend on how the sample is defined. Robustness is therefore reported
as sensitivity ranges: I vary Shopee's assumed rate, exclude each platform in turn, drop the largest
comparison, and restrict the longitudinal result to issuer-reported pairs.

8. Next Steps
The data and empirical framework are assembled. The remaining work will reconcile the definitions
behind the BPS and platform levels, divide movements in the wedge into transaction-volume and
monetization effects, extend the formal test with quarterly pairs where the filings permit, test
alternative sample-inclusion rules, and complete the robustness checks. A later extension can test
which indicator, or which component of revenue growth, is more informative for the stock returns
of the listed platforms, subject to the small and segment-affected sample. Table 8 sets out that
schedule.

Proposal stage

The study treats the choice of indicator as an empirical question. It measures how far the indicators
disagree, tests whether the relationship between revenue and transaction value remains stable, and
identifies which conclusions about the size, growth and direction of digital activity depend on the
indicator chosen.
